stemMd:
Two years ago the district court made mediation compulsory for civil claims under 10,000 euro. Since then the number of such claims reaching trial has fallen by about a third. Compulsory mediation is therefore an effective way of keeping small claims out of the courtroom.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
instructionsMd: Treat each option as true and ask which does most damage to the step from the fall in trials to the claim that mediation caused it.

options.label: A
options.textMd: Mediators in this district are paid less per session than mediators in the neighbouring district, and many work part-time.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Some parties who settled small claims in mediation later complained that the terms they had accepted were unfair to them.

options.label: C
options.textMd: The court has not increased the number of judges assigned to civil claims since mediation became compulsory two years ago.

options.label: D
options.textMd: The court tripled all civil filing fees at the same time, and trials of claims over 10,000 euro also fell by about a third.

explanationMd:
The argument is causal, and it rests on a single piece of evidence: small-claim trials fell by a third after compulsory mediation began. Its unstated step is that mediation is what produced the fall. The way to weaken a causal argument built on before-and-after evidence is to supply a **rival cause** that would have produced the same fall on its own.

The choice about the tripled filing fees and the matching fall among claims over 10,000 euro does exactly that, and does it twice over. It names a change, made at the same time as mediation became compulsory, that plausibly deters filings across the board — tripled filing fees for all civil claims — and then supplies a control group: claims **over** 10,000 euro, which were never subject to compulsory mediation, fell by the same third. If trials fell equally in a category mediation never touched, the fall in the under-10,000 category is no longer evidence that mediation caused anything.

**How to check.** Ask what the argument would have to show to survive each option. Against that choice it would need a reason why the fall in small claims exceeds the fall everywhere else — and by the figures given, it does not. Against the other three it needs nothing at all, because none of them bears on whether mediation caused the fall.

distractorRationale.a: Mediators' pay per session relative to another district, and how many of them work part-time, says nothing about whether claims stopped reaching trial here. It neither supplies a rival cause for the fall nor challenges the figures, so the argument stands untouched.
distractorRationale.b: This attacks the fairness of mediated outcomes, not the claim being argued. The conclusion is that mediation keeps small claims out of the courtroom; settlements that parties later complain about are still settlements, so if anything they are consistent with claims being diverted from trial.
distractorRationale.c: Judge numbers staying flat over the two years removes one alternative explanation rather than supplying one — a court with no extra judges cannot have cleared the caseload by sitting more often. Read carefully, this mildly supports the argument instead of weakening it.

accessibilityText: A weaken question. The argument is that compulsory mediation for civil claims under 10,000 euro is effective, because the number of such claims reaching trial has fallen by about a third in the two years since it was introduced. Four statements follow and the question asks which most weakens the argument.

provenance.notes: Original item written to the published syllabus entry 'identifying the statement that most weakens, or most strengthens, an argument'. The district court, the policy and all figures are invented.

review.author: bocconi-law-topup-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: The tripled filing fees are an alternative cause introduced at the same time, and the equal one-third fall for claims above 10,000 euro (not subject to mediation) shows the drop occurred without mediation. Mediator pay, later complaints of unfair settlements, and the unchanged number of judges do not bear on whether mediation caused the fall in trials. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-cue-batch1-run1) reached the same answer: The tripled filing fees give an alternative cause introduced at the same time, and the equal one-third fall for claims over 10,000 euro, which were not subject to mediation, acts as a control showing the drop is not specific to mediation. Mediator pay, later complaints about settlement fairness, and unchanged judge numbers do not bear on whether mediation caused the fall in trials.]

review.notes: Author checked that only the choice about tripled filing fees bears on the causal step, supplying both a rival cause and an untreated control group. The choice about mediators' pay is irrelevant, the choice about unfair settlements attacks a conclusion the argument does not draw, and the choice about unchanged judge numbers removes a rival cause rather than adding one.
